blocks.p: Now I saw that they went on until they came to the river on this side of the Delectable Mountains: the river where the fine trees grow on both banks, whose leaves, taken inwardly, are good against overindulgence; where the meadows are green all year long, and where they could lie down in safety. [Ps. 23]

Beside this river, in the meadow, there were pens and folds for sheep, and a house built for the nourishing and raising of the lambs, the babies of the women who go on pilgrimage. [Heb. 5:2] There was also One here who had been entrusted with them, who could feel compassion, who could gather these lambs in his arm and carry them in his bosom, and who could gently lead those that were with young. [Isa. 40:11] Christiana urged her four daughters to commit their little ones to the care of this Man, so that by these waters they might be housed, sheltered, cared for, and fed, and so that none of them might be lacking in time to come. If any of them should go astray or be lost, this Man will bring them back again; he will bind up what is broken, and he will strengthen the sick. [Ezek. 34:11-16] Here they will never want for food, drink, or clothing; here they will be kept safe from thieves and robbers; for this Man will die before one of those committed to his trust is lost. [Jer. 23:4]

Besides, here they will be sure of good upbringing and instruction, and will be taught to walk in right paths, which, as you know, is no small favor. And here too, as you see, are sweet waters, pleasant meadows, delicate flowers, and all kinds of trees, the sort that bear wholesome fruit: not fruit like the kind Matthew ate, which fell over the wall out of Beelzebub’s garden, but fruit that brings health where there is none, and keeps it and increases it where there is.

So they were content to commit their little ones to him; and what further encouraged them to do so was that all of this was at the King’s expense, so that it was like a hospital for young children and orphans.

Now they went on; and when they came to By-path Meadow, to the stile over which Christian had gone with his companion Hopeful when they were taken by Giant Despair and put into Doubting Castle, they sat down and considered what was best to be done; that is, now that they were so strong and had such a man as Mr. Great-heart for their guide, whether they had not better make an attempt on the Giant, demolish his castle, and, if there were any pilgrims in it, set them free before they went any further. One said one thing and another the opposite. One asked whether it was lawful to go onto unconsecrated ground; another said they might, provided their purpose was good.

“That last claim cannot be true in every case,” said Mr. Great-heart. “But I have a commandment to resist sin, to overcome evil, and to fight the good fight of faith; and I ask you, with whom should I fight this good fight, if not with Giant Despair? So I will attempt to take his life and to demolish Doubting Castle.” Then he said, “Who will go with me?”
“And so will we,” said Christiana’s four sons, Matthew, Samuel, James, and Joseph; for they were young men, and strong. [1 John 3:13-14]

So they left the women in the road, and with them Mr. Feeble-mind and Mr. Ready-to-stumble with his crutches to be their guard until they came back; for in that place, though Giant Despair lived so near, as long as they kept to the road a little child might have led them. [Isa. 11:6]

So Mr. Great-heart, old Honest, and the four young men went up to Doubting Castle to look for Giant Despair. When they came to the castle gate, they knocked for entrance with an uncommon noise. At that the old Giant came to the gate, with his wife Misgiving following behind him.
“Who and what is he,” said the Giant, “who is so bold as to trouble Giant Despair in this manner?”

“It is I, Great-heart,” Mr. Great-heart replied, “one of the King of the Celestial Country’s guides of pilgrims to their place; and I demand that you open your gates for my entrance. Prepare yourself to fight as well, for I have come to take off your head and to demolish Doubting Castle.”

Now Giant Despair, because he was a giant, thought no man could overcome him; and besides, he thought, since I have conquered angels before now, shall Great-heart make me afraid? So he put on his armor and went out. He had a steel cap on his head, a breastplate of fire strapped on him, iron shoes on his feet, and a great club in his hand. Then these six men came up to him and surrounded him behind and before. And when Misgiving the giantess came up to help him, old Mr. Honest cut her down at a single blow. Then they fought for their lives, and Giant Despair was brought to the ground; but he was very unwilling to die. He struggled hard, and had, as they say, as many lives as a cat; but Great-heart was his death, for he did not leave him until he had severed his head from his shoulders.

Then they set about demolishing Doubting Castle, which, as you know, could be done with ease now that Giant Despair was dead. They were seven days destroying it; and in it they found two pilgrims, a Mr. Despondency, nearly starved to death, and his daughter Much-afraid. These two they saved alive. But it would have made you wonder to see the dead bodies that lay here and there in the castle yard, and how full of dead men’s bones the dungeon was.

When Mr. Great-heart and his companions had done this exploit, they took Mr. Despondency and his daughter Much-afraid under their protection, for they were honest people, even though they had been prisoners of that tyrant Giant Despair in Doubting Castle. They took the Giant’s head with them, for his body they had buried under a heap of stones, and came down to the road and to their companions and showed them what they had done. When Feeble-mind and Ready-to-stumble saw that it really was the head of Giant Despair, they were full of cheer. Now Christiana, when there was call for it, could play the viol, and her daughter Mercy the lute; so, since they were all in such a merry mood, she played them a tune, and Ready-to-stumble would dance. He took Despondency’s daughter Much-afraid by the hand, and off they went, dancing in the road. True, he could not dance without one crutch in his hand, but I promise you he footed it well. And the girl deserved credit too, for she answered the music handsomely.

As for Mr. Despondency, the music was not much to him; he was for eating rather than dancing, for he was nearly starved. So Christiana gave him some of her bottle of spirits for immediate relief, and then prepared him something to eat; and in a little while the old gentleman came to himself and began to be finely revived.

Now I saw in my dream that when all these things were finished, Mr. Great-heart took the head of Giant Despair and set it on a pole by the roadside, right across from the pillar that Christian had put up to warn the pilgrims who came after him against entering the Giant’s grounds.

v: Though Doubting Castle has been razed, and though
the Giant Despair has lost his head,
sin can rebuild it, make the walls regrow,
and make Despair live on, who now lies dead.

blocks.p: Then he wrote these verses beneath it on a marble stone:

v: This is the head of one whose name alone
once made the pilgrims tremble to the bone.
His castle’s down; Misgiving too, his wife,
brave Master Great-heart has bereft of life.
Great-heart has rescued from the giant’s slaughter.
Who doubts it, let him look up here and see
this head, and let his doubting cease to be.
And when the lame and fearful dance below,
this head declares their fears have let them go.

blocks.p: When these men had shown themselves so bravely against Doubting Castle and had slain Giant Despair, they went forward, and went on until they came to the Delectable Mountains, where Christian and Hopeful had refreshed themselves with the variety of the place. They also made themselves known to the shepherds there, who welcomed them to the Delectable Mountains as they had welcomed Christian before them.
